CAS Monograph 15 is *Introduction to Capital Modeling and Portfolio
Management* (John Major and Stephen Mildenhall, 2026). Its chapter 8 covers
four advanced topics: parameter uncertainty, the Iman-Conover method to
correlate simulated units, capital allocation by layer, and Bodoff's layer
allocation. This guide runs each topic in prospicio from R and prints the
monograph's numbers beside prospicio's.

This is the R twin of the Python guide
[`capital-modeling-monograph-15-iman-conover.md`](capital-modeling-monograph-15-iman-conover.md),
with the same sections and numbers. The R package calls the same Rust code as
the Python package. So the seeded samples, the Iman-Conover shuffles and every
printed value agree with the Python guide.

The chapter has two kinds of number. Some are exact, for example the regional
means and percentiles of Example 2 (computed by FFT) and every InsCo table in
sections 8.3 and 8.4. These should agree with prospicio to the printed digits.
Others come from one random sample of 1,000 simulations, for example the
achieved correlations of Examples 1 and 2. prospicio draws its own sample, so
these numbers agree only within sampling error, and the guide shows the size
of that error. The explanations are in new words, and the table numbers are
the monograph's.

The text block after each R chunk is the output of that chunk.
`R/prospicio/tests/test-guides.R` runs the chunks in order and checks that
each chunk prints exactly that text.

Companion guides: [chapter 9](capital-modeling-monograph-15.qmd), [chapters 3
and 4](capital-modeling-monograph-15-theory.qmd), [chapters 5 and
6](capital-modeling-monograph-15-applications.qmd) and [chapters 1, 2 and
7](capital-modeling-monograph-15-practice.qmd).

## 1. Parameter uncertainty

Section 8.1 separates process risk (the randomness of a loss with a known
distribution) from parameter uncertainty (an unknown distribution). It gives
four responses: ignore the uncertainty, report a range, absorb it into a
predictive distribution, or isolate a credible worst case. Take a lognormal
severity with a shape `sigma` of 1.2 and an expected value of about 100. Its
log-scale location is known only to within 0.3 in each direction. The code
shows what each response does to the 99.5% quantile:

```{r}
library(prospicio)

SIGMA <- 1.2
best <- log(100) - SIGMA^2 / 2
severities <- lapply(c(-0.3, 0, 0.3), function(shift) lognormal(best + shift, SIGMA))

mixture_quantile <- function(dists, p, lo = 0, hi = 1e6) {
  # The p quantile of an equal mixture, by bisection on its cdf.
  for (i in 1:200) {
    mid <- (lo + hi) / 2
    if (mean(sapply(dists, function(d) cdf(d, mid))) < p) lo <- mid else hi <- mid
  }
  (lo + hi) / 2
}

for (d in severities) {
  cat(sprintf("report it:   mean %5.1f, 99.5%% quantile %6.1f\n", mean(d), quantile(d, 0.995)))
}
cat(sprintf("ignore it:                     99.5%% quantile %6.1f\n", quantile(severities[[2]], 0.995)))
cat(sprintf("absorb it:                     99.5%% quantile %6.1f\n", mixture_quantile(severities, 0.995)))
cat(sprintf("isolate it:                    99.5%% quantile %6.1f\n", quantile(severities[[3]], 0.995)))
```

```text
report it:   mean  74.1, 99.5% quantile  793.3
report it:   mean 100.0, 99.5% quantile 1070.8
report it:   mean 135.0, 99.5% quantile 1445.4
ignore it:                     99.5% quantile 1070.8
absorb it:                     99.5% quantile 1139.9
isolate it:                    99.5% quantile 1445.4
```

Reporting gives a range, here from about 790 to 1,450. Absorbing the
uncertainty, with equal weights on the three locations, gives one answer about
6% above the best estimate. The wider spread of the mixture increases its
quantile. This is the downward bias that the monograph mentions in a quantile
that ignores parameter uncertainty. Isolating a worst case gives the highest
answer.

In prospicio, `blend_predictive()` does the same mixing of whole simulations:
it takes each simulation from one of several models with given weights. The
Bayesian models (for example `bayes_odp()` in reserving) return predictive
distributions that already include parameter uncertainty.

## 2. Example 1: three units

Section 8.2.2 correlates three units: Auto, GL and Property. Each unit has a
lognormal severity limited per occurrence and a gamma-mixed Poisson count:

| Unit | Expected loss | Limit | Severity mean | Severity CV | Mixing CV |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Auto | 5,000 | 2,000 | 30 | 2 | 0.2 |
| GL | 2,000 | 5,000 | 50 | 5 | 0.3 |
| Property | 7,000 | 10,000 | 100 | 5 | 0.1 |

prospicio compounds each unit by FFT. Then `copula_simulate()` with an
independence (identity) Gaussian copula draws 1,000 independent years from the
three distributions, as the monograph does:

```{r}
unit <- function(loss, limit, mean, cv, mixing_cv, step = 1, points = 2^16) {
  # A unit's annual loss: limited lognormal claims, gamma-mixed Poisson count.
  severity <- discretize(lognormal_from_mean_cv(mean, cv), step, points, "local_moment")
  claim <- map_grid(severity, function(x) pmin(x, limit))$grid
  compound_distribution(mixed_poisson_count(loss / mean(claim), mixing_cv), claim, points,
                        method = "fft")
}

UNITS <- list(Auto = c(5000, 2000, 30, 2, 0.2), GL = c(2000, 5000, 50, 5, 0.3),
              Property = c(7000, 10000, 100, 5, 0.1))
grids <- lapply(UNITS, function(a) do.call(unit, as.list(a)))
KEYS <- data.frame(unit = names(UNITS))
IDENTITY <- diag(3)
sample <- copula_simulate(gaussian_copula(IDENTITY), grids, 1000, 815, keys = KEYS)
X <- draw_matrix(sample)

BOOK_81 <- list(Auto = c(5011.7, 0.257), GL = c(2092.4, 0.660), Property = c(7117.8, 0.467))
cat(sprintf("%-9s %9s %7s %12s %6s   book sample\n", "", "FFT mean", "FFT cv", "sample mean", "cv"))
for (j in seq_along(UNITS)) {
  g <- grids[[j]]
  cat(sprintf("%-9s %9.1f %7.3f %12.1f %6.3f   (%s)\n", names(UNITS)[j], mean(g),
              sqrt(variance(g)) / mean(g), mean(X[, j]), sd(X[, j]) / mean(X[, j]),
              paste(BOOK_81[[j]], collapse = ", ")))
}
```

```text
           FFT mean  FFT cv  sample mean     cv   book sample
Auto         5000.0   0.262       4998.8  0.262   (5011.7, 0.257)
GL           2000.0   0.672       2042.0  0.644   (2092.4, 0.66)
Property     7000.0   0.465       7017.0  0.454   (7117.8, 0.467)
```

The FFT means are the requested 5,000, 2,000 and 7,000, and the CVs are those
of the model. Table 8.1 of the monograph describes its own sample, with means
of 5,011.7, 2,092.4 and 7,117.8 and CVs of 0.257, 0.660 and 0.467. The
prospicio sample differs from it by about as much as each sample differs from
the model. These are sampling differences of a few percent, not model
differences.

## 3. The target and the achieved correlation

The target (Table 8.2) has a correlation of -0.3 between Auto and GL, 0.8
between GL and Property, and 0 between Auto and Property. A target must be a
correlation matrix, that is, symmetric and positive definite. prospicio
refuses a target that is not:

```{r}
TARGET <- rbind(c(1, -0.3, 0), c(-0.3, 1, 0.8), c(0, 0.8, 1))
cat("eigenvalues of the target:", sprintf("%.3f", sort(eigen(TARGET, symmetric = TRUE)$values)), "\n")
bad <- rbind(c(1, 0.9, 0.9), c(0.9, 1, -0.9), c(0.9, -0.9, 1))
tryCatch(iman_conover(sample, bad, 1), error = function(e) cat("not positive definite: error\n"))
```

```text
eigenvalues of the target: 0.146 1.000 1.854 
not positive definite: error
```

`iman_conover()` reorders each column of the sample. Each unit keeps exactly
its own 1,000 values, and only the grouping of the values into years changes.
The code computes the achieved correlations of Table 8.3. It ranks ties in
order of appearance (`rank(ties.method = "first")`), as the Python guide does:

```{r}
PAIRS <- list(c(1, 2), c(1, 3), c(2, 3))
NAMES <- c("Auto-GL", "Auto-Property", "GL-Property")

ranks <- function(m) apply(as.matrix(m), 2, rank, ties.method = "first")

pairs_of <- function(m) {
  # Pearson and Spearman correlation of each pair of columns.
  pearson <- cor(m)
  spearman <- cor(ranks(m))
  lapply(PAIRS, function(p) c(pearson[p[1], p[2]], spearman[p[1], p[2]]))
}

joint <- iman_conover(sample, TARGET, 1)
Y <- draw_matrix(joint)
cat("marginals unchanged:", all(sapply(1:3, function(j) identical(sort(X[, j]), sort(Y[, j])))), "\n")
BOOK_83 <- list(c(-0.271, -0.287), c(0.003, 0.003), c(0.772, 0.779)) # (linear, rank)
cat(sprintf("%-14s %7s %8s %7s %9s %7s\n", "", "target", "Pearson", "book", "Spearman", "book"))
got <- pairs_of(Y)
for (k in 1:3) {
  p <- PAIRS[[k]]
  cat(sprintf("%-14s %7.1f %8.3f %7.3f %9.3f %7.3f\n", NAMES[k], TARGET[p[1], p[2]],
              got[[k]][1], BOOK_83[[k]][1], got[[k]][2], BOOK_83[[k]][2]))
}
```

```text
marginals unchanged: TRUE 
                target  Pearson    book  Spearman    book
Auto-GL           -0.3   -0.278  -0.271    -0.270  -0.287
Auto-Property      0.0   -0.002   0.003     0.003   0.003
GL-Property        0.8    0.773   0.772     0.784   0.779
```

The pattern is the monograph's: Auto-GL and GL-Property land a little inside
the target, and Auto-Property stays near zero. The digits differ because the
samples and the shuffles differ. To show how much a sample of 1,000 moves
them, the code repeats the calculation with 100 different samples and
shuffles:

```{r}
runs <- array(0, c(100, 3, 2)) # run, pair, (Pearson, Spearman)
for (s in 0:99) {
  draw <- copula_simulate(gaussian_copula(IDENTITY), grids, 1000, 1000 + s, keys = KEYS)
  got <- pairs_of(draw_matrix(iman_conover(draw, TARGET, s)))
  for (k in 1:3) runs[s + 1, k, ] <- got[[k]]
}
f3 <- function(v) sub("^-0\\.000$", "0.000", sprintf("%.3f", v))
cat(sprintf("%-14s %11s %7s %7s %12s %7s %7s\n", "", "Pearson 5%", "mean", "95%",
            "Spearman 5%", "mean", "95%"))
for (k in 1:3) {
  pe <- runs[, k, 1]
  sp <- runs[, k, 2]
  cells <- f3(c(quantile(pe, 0.05), mean(pe), quantile(pe, 0.95),
                quantile(sp, 0.05), mean(sp), quantile(sp, 0.95)))
  cat(sprintf("%-14s %11s %7s %7s %12s %7s %7s\n", NAMES[k], cells[1], cells[2], cells[3],
              cells[4], cells[5], cells[6]))
}
gauss <- sapply(PAIRS, function(p) round(6 / pi * asin(TARGET[p[1], p[2]] / 2), 3))
cat("Gaussian Spearman (6/pi) asin(r/2):", sprintf("%.3f", gauss), "\n")
```

```text
                Pearson 5%    mean     95%  Spearman 5%    mean     95%
Auto-GL             -0.286  -0.269  -0.252       -0.298  -0.286  -0.271
Auto-Property       -0.020   0.000   0.021       -0.012   0.000   0.016
GL-Property          0.752   0.773   0.791        0.778   0.787   0.795
Gaussian Spearman (6/pi) asin(r/2): -0.288 0.000 0.786 
```

Every value of Table 8.3 is inside these 90% ranges. So the monograph's sample
and the prospicio sample agree as far as a sample of 1,000 can show. Two
results are not sampling error:

- **The rank correlation is the Gaussian rank correlation of the target.**
  prospicio gives the reference scores exactly the target correlation, and
  Iman-Conover copies their ranks. So Spearman's rho is near `(6/pi)
  asin(r/2)`, the rank correlation of a bivariate normal with correlation `r`.
  That gives -0.288 for -0.3 and 0.786 for 0.8. The monograph's -0.287 and
  0.779 are within sampling distance of these values.
- **The linear correlation is less than the target.** Pearson's correlation
  depends on the marginals. Skewed marginals cannot reach a high linear
  correlation, even when their ranks agree perfectly. The maximum for GL and
  Property is the correlation of the two samples sorted together:

```{r}
bounds <- function(a, b) {
  # The largest and smallest Pearson correlation any pairing of a and b can have.
  c(cor(sort(a), sort(b)), cor(sort(a), rev(sort(b))))
}
b <- bounds(X[, 2], X[, 3])
cat(sprintf("GL-Property: at most %.3f, at least %.3f\n", b[1], b[2]))
b <- bounds(X[, 1], X[, 2])
cat(sprintf("Auto-GL:     at most %.3f, at least %.3f\n", b[1], b[2]))
```

```text
GL-Property: at most 0.997, at least -0.779
Auto-GL:     at most 0.963, at least -0.890
```

This maximum is the reason for the monograph's warning that a request for a
very high correlation can disappoint. When Pearson's correlation is important,
set the input a little above the output you need. Or use the rank correlation,
which Iman-Conover controls directly.

## 4. The output's row order

Section 8.2.5 of the monograph compares methods. Its item 6 warns that some
implementations return the rows of an Iman-Conover sample in a systematic
order, so you must use the sample whole. The prospicio implementation does
this. The first column of its reference holds the scores in increasing order,
so prospicio returns the first unit sorted:

```{r}
cat("Auto sorted ascending:", all(diff(Y[, 1]) >= 0), "\n")
cat(sprintf("mean of the first 100 years: Auto %7.1f  (all 1,000: %7.1f)\n",
            mean(Y[1:100, 1]), mean(Y[, 1])))
u <- copula_sample(gaussian_copula(IDENTITY), 1000, 99)
shuffled <- Y[order(u[, 1]), ]
cat(sprintf("after a random row order:     Auto %7.1f\n", mean(shuffled[1:100, 1])))
```

```text
Auto sorted ascending: TRUE 
mean of the first 100 years: Auto  2965.4  (all 1,000:  4998.8)
after a random row order:     Auto  4856.5
```

So the first 100 rows of the output are not a random sample of 100 years.
Statistics over all rows (means, quantiles, a `capital_portfolio()` built from
them) do not depend on the row order. Shuffle the rows, as above, before you
take a subset or pair the output row by row with another simulation.

## 5. The algorithm by hand

Section 8.2.8 derives the method in four steps:

1. Take `n` scores with mean 0 and variance 1. The monograph prefers the
   evenly spaced normal quantiles `Phi^-1(i / (n + 1))`.
2. Put an independently permuted copy of the scores in each of `m` columns to
   make `M`. Then `M'M / n` is close to the identity.
3. Let `S = C'C` be the Cholesky factorization of the target, and `M'M / n =
   F'F` that of the actual correlation of `M`. Then `T = M F^-1 C` has
   correlation exactly `S`.
4. Give each column of the input the rank order of the matching column of `T`.

The code does this in a dozen lines (`chol()` returns the upper triangular
factor):

```{r}
iman_conover_by_hand <- function(x, target, scores, seed) {
  n <- nrow(x)
  m <- ncol(x)
  scores <- (scores - mean(scores)) / sqrt(mean((scores - mean(scores))^2))
  u <- copula_sample(gaussian_copula(diag(m)), n, seed)
  M <- sapply(1:m, function(j) scores[order(u[, j])])
  F <- chol(crossprod(M) / n) # upper triangular, M'M/n = F'F
  C <- chol(target)
  T <- M %*% solve(F) %*% C
  out <- sapply(1:m, function(j) sort(x[, j])[rank(T[, j], ties.method = "first")])
  list(out = out, M = M, T = T)
}

n <- 1000
normal_scores <- qnorm(seq_len(n) / (n + 1))
by_hand <- iman_conover_by_hand(X, TARGET, normal_scores, 3)
M <- by_hand$M
T <- by_hand$T
cat(sprintf("largest error of M'M/n against the identity: %.3f\n", max(abs(crossprod(M) / n - diag(3)))))
cat("T'T/n equals the target to 1e-12:", max(abs(crossprod(T) / n - TARGET)) < 1e-12, "\n")
cat("by hand,   Spearman:", sprintf("%.3f", sapply(pairs_of(by_hand$out), `[`, 2)), "\n")
cat("prospicio, Spearman:", sprintf("%.3f", sapply(pairs_of(Y), `[`, 2)), "\n")
```

```text
largest error of M'M/n against the identity: 0.035
T'T/n equals the target to 1e-12: TRUE 
by hand,   Spearman: -0.281 -0.002 0.788 
prospicio, Spearman: -0.270 0.003 0.784 
```

The random permutations alone leave errors of a few hundredths in the
correlation of `M`, and the `F^-1` step removes them. The two results are not
equal row by row, because the permutations differ. But both have the
correlation structure of a normal reference with the target correlation.

## 6. Other reference distributions and copulas

Section 8.2.3 replaces the normal scores with Student t scores, which put more
weight on joint extremes. The function `iman_conover_by_hand` above takes any
scores. The t distribution with 2 degrees of freedom is the extreme example of
the monograph. Its quantile has the closed form `(2u - 1) / sqrt(2 u (1 -
u))`. The code counts how often GL and Property are both in their worst 1% of
10,000 years under each reference:

```{r}
n <- 10000
draws <- draw_matrix(copula_simulate(gaussian_copula(IDENTITY), grids, n, 4, keys = KEYS))
uu <- seq_len(n) / (n + 1)
SCORES <- list(normal = qnorm(uu), "t, 2 dof" = (2 * uu - 1) / sqrt(2 * uu * (1 - uu)))
for (name in names(SCORES)) {
  Z <- iman_conover_by_hand(draws, TARGET, SCORES[[name]], 5)$out
  r <- ranks(Z) - 1
  worst <- (r[, 2] >= 0.99 * n) & (r[, 3] >= 0.99 * n)
  cat(sprintf("%-9s GL-Property Spearman %.3f, years in both worst 1%%: %d\n", name,
              pairs_of(Z)[[3]][2], sum(worst)))
}
cat("if independent, about", n %/% 10000, "\n")
```

```text
normal    GL-Property Spearman 0.787, years in both worst 1%: 34
t, 2 dof  GL-Property Spearman 0.714, years in both worst 1%: 68
if independent, about 1 
```

With t scores the joint extremes are about twice as frequent, although the
overall rank correlation is lower. This is the pinched scatter of Figure 8.3
of the monograph. The monograph also warns that this flexibility is not a
reason to use it.

Section 8.2.4 asks if a copula can be the reference. A multivariate
Archimedean copula has a single parameter and cannot match a correlation
matrix, as the monograph says. You can instead use the prospicio copulas to
simulate directly (`copula_simulate()` with `gaussian_copula()`, `t_copula()`,
`archimedean_copula()`, `nested_archimedean_copula()` or `vine_copula()`). The
nested Archimedean copulas and the C- and D-vines avoid the limit of a single
parameter. A vine builds the joint distribution from one bivariate copula per
edge, so it can have a different strength and tail for each pair.

## 7. Iman-Conover against the normal copula

The normal copula method (section 8.2.5) simulates each year. It draws
correlated normals and transforms each one to the distribution of its unit
through the quantile function. With normal scores, Iman-Conover does the same
to a sample that already exists, with one difference: it corrects the
reference to the exact correlation. The code repeats both methods 100 times on
the same units to show the effect of that correction:

```{r}
normal_copula <- gaussian_copula(TARGET)
spread <- list("Iman-Conover" = numeric(), "normal copula" = numeric())
for (s in 0:99) {
  draw <- copula_simulate(gaussian_copula(IDENTITY), grids, 1000, 3000 + s, keys = KEYS)
  spread[[1]] <- c(spread[[1]], pairs_of(draw_matrix(iman_conover(draw, TARGET, s)))[[3]][2])
  copula_draw <- copula_simulate(normal_copula, grids, 1000, 5000 + s, keys = KEYS)
  spread[[2]] <- c(spread[[2]], pairs_of(draw_matrix(copula_draw))[[3]][2])
}
for (name in names(spread)) {
  v <- spread[[name]]
  cat(sprintf("%-14s GL-Property Spearman: mean %.3f, sd %.4f\n", name, mean(v),
              sqrt(mean((v - mean(v))^2))))
}
```

```text
Iman-Conover   GL-Property Spearman: mean 0.787, sd 0.0052
normal copula  GL-Property Spearman: mean 0.787, sd 0.0142
```

Both methods centre on the Gaussian rank correlation of about 0.786. The
correlation of the normal copula varies from sample to sample, as any sample
statistic does. The correlation of Iman-Conover varies much less, because only
the small gap between the rank and linear correlations of the normal reference
remains. But the normal copula makes one independent year at a time, so you
can split, subset or extend its output freely. An Iman-Conover sample is made
in one piece from inputs that already exist, and it needs the care of section
4.

## 8. Example 2: block Iman-Conover

A large correlation matrix estimated from data is mostly noise. The block
Iman-Conover of section 8.2.6 uses the correlations that data can estimate.
These are a correlation between lines within each region and a correlation
between the region totals.

Example 2 (section 8.2.7) has four regions, each with Auto (AL), GL and
Property (Pr). Each line has the same model as in Example 1, except that the
GL severity CV is 4. The first step computes the region totals with
independent lines, by FFT, as in Table 8.4. A `capital_portfolio()` built from
a named list of grids convolves them (Python's `Portfolio.from_independent`):

```{r}
LINES <- list(AL = c(2000, 30, 2, 0.2), GL = c(5000, 50, 4, 0.3), Pr = c(10000, 100, 5, 0.1))
REGIONS <- list(North = c(4000, 2000, 2000), East = c(3000, 1000, 3000),
                South = c(5000, 2000, 7000), West = c(5000, 2000, 2000))
BOOK_84 <- list(North = c(8000, 0.298, 16237), East = c(7000, 0.347, 15920),
                South = c(14000, 0.266, 25737), West = c(9000, 0.276, 17331))
region_grids <- lapply(REGIONS, function(losses) {
  stats::setNames(lapply(seq_along(LINES), function(k) {
    do.call(unit, as.list(c(losses[k], LINES[[k]])))
  }), names(LINES))
})
cat(sprintf("%-6s %8s %6s %9s   book\n", "", "mean", "cv", "99th pct"))
for (r in names(REGIONS)) {
  total <- capital_portfolio(region_grids[[r]])
  xs <- total@totals
  ps <- total@probs
  m <- sum(xs * ps)
  cv <- sqrt(sum((xs - m)^2 * ps)) / m
  cat(sprintf("%-6s %8.1f %6.3f %9.0f   (%s)\n", r, m, cv, portfolio_assets(total, 0.99),
              paste(BOOK_84[[r]], collapse = ", ")))
}
```

```text
           mean     cv  99th pct   book
North    8000.0  0.298     16236   (8000, 0.298, 16237)
East     7000.0  0.347     15920   (7000, 0.347, 15920)
South   14000.0  0.266     25737   (14000, 0.266, 25737)
West     9000.0  0.276     17330   (9000, 0.276, 17331)
```

The means and CVs agree to the printed digits. The 99th percentiles agree
within 1.5 in 16,000 to 26,000. They move by that much with the discretization
step (a step of 0.5 gives 16,236.5, 15,920.5, 25,737 and 17,329.5). So the
remaining difference comes from the grid, not the model.

The block method then has three steps:

1. Correlate the lines within each region by ordinary Iman-Conover. Here every
   region has the same 3 x 3 matrix (Table 8.6 (e)), but each region can have
   its own matrix.
2. Stack the regions into one `predictive_distribution()` with a `region`
   dimension (`join_predictive()`).
3. Correlate the region totals: move the years of each region as whole rows,
   which keeps the structure within the region.

The prospicio function `reorder_groups()` does the last step:

```{r}
INTRA <- rbind(c(1, 0.6, 0.2), c(0.6, 1, 0.4), c(0.2, 0.4, 1))
INTER <- rbind(c(1, 0.7, 0.2, 0), c(0.7, 1, 0.4, 0.2), c(0.2, 0.4, 1, 0.8), c(0, 0.2, 0.8, 1))
parts <- list()
for (k in seq_along(region_grids)) {
  r <- names(region_grids)[k]
  draw <- copula_simulate(gaussian_copula(IDENTITY), region_grids[[r]], 1000, 100 + k - 1,
                          keys = data.frame(line = names(LINES)))
  parts[[r]] <- iman_conover(draw, INTRA, k - 1)
}
stacked <- join_predictive(parts, "region")
bic <- reorder_groups(stacked, "region", INTER, 7)
keys <- bic@keys
cat(bic@dims, "|", paste0(keys$region, "/", keys$line)[1:4], "...\n")

B <- draw_matrix(bic)
totals <- sapply(1:4, function(k) rowSums(B[, (3 * k - 2):(3 * k)]))
achieved <- cor(totals)
BOOK_85 <- rbind(c(1, 2, 0.683), c(1, 3, 0.167), c(1, 4, -0.002), c(2, 3, 0.369),
                 c(2, 4, 0.197), c(3, 4, 0.799))
names_r <- names(REGIONS)
cat(sprintf("%-12s %7s %9s %7s\n", "", "target", "achieved", "book"))
for (row in seq_len(nrow(BOOK_85))) {
  i <- BOOK_85[row, 1]
  j <- BOOK_85[row, 2]
  cat(sprintf("%-12s %7.1f %9.3f %7.3f\n", paste0(names_r[i], "-", names_r[j]), INTER[i, j],
              achieved[i, j], BOOK_85[row, 3]))
}
```

The full 12 x 12 matrix (Table 8.7) has the block structure of Figure 8.4 of

## 9. Capital by layer, if you must

Section 8.3 returns to InsCo (ten equally likely years, three units) and its
Wang distortion calibrated to a 15% return with assets of 100. It divides the
assets into layers between consecutive distinct totals. In each layer, `alpha`
shares the expected loss between units. `alpha` is the expected share of each
unit in the total, in the years that reach the layer. `beta` shares the
premium in the same way, under the distorted probabilities. A layer's margin
is its premium less its loss, and its capital is the part of its width that
premium does not fund.

The cost of capital in a layer, `iota = (g(S) - S) / (1 - g(S))`, is the same
for every unit. So the capital of a unit in a layer is its margin there
divided by `iota` (equation 8.5).

```{r}
ROWS <- rbind(
  c(15, 7, 0), c(15, 13, 0), c(5, 20, 11), c(7, 33, 0), c(13, 20, 7),
  c(5, 27, 8), c(15, 16, 9), c(26, 19, 10), c(17, 8, 40), c(16, 20, 64)
)
colnames(ROWS) <- c("A", "B", "C")
insco <- capital_portfolio(ROWS)
wang <- calibrate_portfolio(insco, "wang", assets = 100, return_on_capital = 0.15)

layers <- function(port, g) {
  # Per layer: bottom, width, S, g(S), iota, and per unit alpha S, beta g(S),
  # margin and capital, all per unit of width.
  x <- c(0, port@totals)
  p <- port@probs
  nl <- length(p)
  share <- sapply(port@units, function(u) portfolio_kappa(port, u) / port@totals)
  S <- c(1, pmax(0, 1 - cumsum(p)))
  G <- sapply(S, function(s) distortion_g(g, s))
  q <- G[1:nl] - G[2:(nl + 1)]
  lapply(1:nl, function(k) {
    idx <- k:nl
    aS <- colSums(p[idx] * share[idx, , drop = FALSE])
    bG <- colSums(q[idx] * share[idx, , drop = FALSE])
    margin <- bG - aS
    iota <- if (G[k] < 1) (G[k] - S[k]) / (1 - G[k]) else NA
    capital <- if (is.na(iota)) rep(0, length(margin)) else margin / iota
    list(x = x[k], dx = x[k + 1] - x[k], S = S[k], g = G[k], iota = iota, aS = aS, bG = bG,
         margin = margin, capital = capital)
  })
}

cat(sprintf("%4s %3s %4s %6s %6s %20s   %20s\n", "x", "dx", "S", "g(S)", "iota",
            "margin A, B, C", "capital A, B, C"))
for (l in layers(insco, wang)) {
  it <- if (is.na(l$iota)) "     -" else sprintf("%6.3f", l$iota)
  cat(sprintf("%4.0f %3.0f %4.1f %6.3f %s %s   %s\n", l$x, l$dx, l$S, l$g, it,
              paste(sprintf("%6.3f", l$margin), collapse = " "),
              paste(sprintf("%6.3f", l$capital), collapse = " ")))
}
```

```text
   x  dx    S   g(S)   iota       margin A, B, C        capital A, B, C
   0  22  1.0  1.000      - -0.030 -0.032  0.061    0.000  0.000  0.000
  22   6  0.9  0.948  0.917  0.003 -0.017  0.061    0.003 -0.018  0.067
  28   8  0.8  0.882  0.693  0.021 -0.001  0.061    0.031 -0.001  0.089
  36   4  0.7  0.807  0.555  0.025  0.013  0.069    0.045  0.024  0.125
  40  15  0.3  0.428  0.224  0.030  0.026  0.072    0.134  0.115  0.323
  55  10  0.2  0.309  0.158  0.021  0.019  0.069    0.133  0.121  0.437
  65  35  0.1  0.174  0.089  0.012  0.015  0.047    0.132  0.165  0.529
```

These values are Table 8.10 (with `g(S)` from Table 8.9), per unit of layer
width, and agree with it to the printed digits. The code keeps `alpha S` and
`beta g(S)`, the columns of Tables 8.8 and 8.9, for section 10. Losses in
every year pay for the bottom layer, from 0 to 22. So that layer needs no
capital, and `iota` is undefined there. Its unit margins sum to zero and are
cross-subsidies between the units. The sum of each column times the layer
width gives the margin and capital of each unit:

```{r}
by_unit <- function(port, g) {
  ls <- layers(port, g)
  list(margin = Reduce(`+`, lapply(ls, function(l) l$dx * l$margin)),
       capital = Reduce(`+`, lapply(ls, function(l) l$dx * l$capital)))
}
units_only <- function(priced) priced[priced$unit != "total", ]

bu <- by_unit(insco, wang)
lifted <- units_only(natural_price(insco, wang, assets = 100, allocation = "lifted"))
cat("margin   ", sprintf("%.3f", bu$margin), " book 0.709 0.337 5.919\n")
cat("capital  ", sprintf("%.3f", bu$capital), " book 8.411 8.691 29.333\n")
cat("natural_price", sprintf("%.3f", lifted$capital), "\n")
cat("return   ", sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * bu$margin / bu$capital),
    sprintf("total %.1f%%", 100 * sum(bu$margin) / sum(bu$capital)), " book 8.4%, 3.9%, 20.2%, 15.0%\n")
```

```text
margin    0.709 0.337 5.919  book 0.709 0.337 5.919
capital   8.411 8.691 29.333  book 8.411 8.691 29.333
natural_price 8.411 8.691 29.333 
return    8.4% 3.9% 20.2% total 15.0%  book 8.4%, 3.9%, 20.2%, 15.0%
```

The returns differ by unit (A earns 8.4%, C 20.2%), although every layer pays
the same return to every unit. The reason is that the units use different
layers. The low layers are expensive but mostly funded by premium, and the
high layers are cheap but mostly capital. `natural_price(..., allocation =
"lifted")` gives the same capital.

Table 8.11 compares this result with the CCoC distortion, where the numbers
depend on the treatment of the bottom layer. Equation 8.5 as written gives the
bottom layer no capital. prospicio, like `aggregate` 1.0.1, converts the
margins of the bottom layer at the limit of `iota` as `S` rises to 1. That
limit is `r = 0.15` for the CCoC and `(1 - rho) / rho` for the proportional
hazard. For the Wang, dual power and TVaR distortions the limit is infinite,
and the two conventions agree. The printed capital of the monograph for these
two families comes from an earlier `aggregate` and matches neither convention:

```{r}
BOOK_Q <- list(ccoc = c(4.874, 5.288, 36.273), ph = c(7.074, 6.565, 32.796))
for (family in c("ccoc", "ph")) {
  d <- calibrate_portfolio(insco, family, assets = 100, return_on_capital = 0.15)
  eq85 <- by_unit(insco, d)$capital
  got <- units_only(natural_price(insco, d, assets = 100, allocation = "lifted"))$capital
  cat(sprintf("%-4s equation 8.5 %s  prospicio %s  book %s\n", family,
              paste(sprintf("%.3f", eq85), collapse = " "), paste(sprintf("%.3f", got), collapse = " "),
              paste(sprintf("%.3f", BOOK_Q[[family]]), collapse = " ")))
}
```

```text
ccoc equation 8.5 5.419 6.082 34.934  prospicio 2.261 1.478 42.696  book 4.874 5.288 36.273
ph   equation 8.5 7.765 7.694 30.975  prospicio 6.481 5.597 34.356  book 7.074 6.565 32.796
```

All three sum to the same total capital of 46.435. They differ only in how
they spread the cross-subsidies of the bottom layer, which sum to zero. Under
the prospicio convention, every unit earns exactly 15% under the CCoC. That is
what a constant cost of capital means (see section 5 of the [chapter 9
guide](capital-modeling-monograph-15.qmd)). The monograph advises against any
allocation of capital, and this result is one more reason.

## 10. Bodoff's layer allocation

Section 8.4 compares the natural allocation with the allocation of Bodoff
(2007). Bodoff shares every layer of the assets by `alpha`, not only its
expected loss. Table 8.12:

```{r}
bodoff <- bodoff_allocation(insco, assets = 100)
cat("Bodoff assets", sprintf("%.3f", bodoff), " total", sprintf("%.1f", sum(bodoff)), "\n")
cat("book          24.159 29.756 46.086  total 100.0\n")
first <- layers(insco, wang)[[1]]
cat("layer 0 to 22:", sprintf("%.3f", first$dx * first$aS / first$S), " book 7.152 9.694 5.154\n")
```

```text
Bodoff assets 24.159 29.756 46.086  total 100.0 
book          24.159 29.756 46.086  total 100.0
layer 0 to 22: 7.152 9.694 5.154  book 7.152 9.694 5.154
```

Bodoff's allocation splits the assets but not the premium. The monograph adds
a CCoC to get a premium. In each layer the premium is the expected loss plus a
margin of `d = r / (1 + r)` on the unfunded part, `alpha (S + d (1 - S))`.
This is the CCoC `g(S)` shared by the loss shares:

```{r}
ccoc <- distortion("ccoc", 0.15)
ls <- Filter(function(l) l$S > 0, layers(insco, ccoc))
bodoff_premium <- Reduce(`+`, lapply(ls, function(l) l$dx * l$g * l$aS / l$S))
natural <- units_only(natural_price(insco, ccoc, assets = 100))$premium
cat("Bodoff with CCoC", sprintf("%.3f", bodoff_premium), sprintf("%.3f", sum(bodoff_premium)), "\n")
cat("natural CCoC    ", sprintf("%.3f", natural), sprintf("%.3f", sum(natural)), "\n")
```

```text
Bodoff with CCoC 14.803 19.794 18.968 53.565 
natural CCoC     13.739 18.522 21.304 53.565 
```

The totals are the same 53.565, but the splits differ. Bodoff's shares are the
expected loss shares in every layer. The natural allocation uses the distorted
shares, which move premium toward the unit that dominates the years to which
the distortion gives more weight (C). A different distortion in place of the
CCoC gives different splits. This is the monograph's point: Bodoff's method
needs one more assumption before it can price anything.
